direction.question: Can interpretability methods support ex ante predictions of durable model-control interventions, including composition, persistence, and bounded side effects across models and tasks?
direction.closureCriteria: Before applying each intervention, predict its target effect, collateral effects, interactions with other interventions, and persistence after additional training or context shifts; beat non-mechanistic baselines across multiple model families and seeds; and reproduce the prediction-to-control mapping independently.
partialResults: Activation steering, representation engineering, sparse autoencoders, causal tracing, and model editing can alter behavior. AxBench finds simple prompting and fine-tuning baselines often beat sparse-autoencoder steering, while localization-versus-editing studies show that causal localization does not reliably identify the best place to edit. Early 2026 work predicts some steering side effects, but results remain method-, dictionary-, and model-dependent.
starters: Individual: On two open small models, use AxBench and CounterFact to predict target and collateral changes before each intervention, then publish calibration curves and all failed predictions.

Small lab: Build a cross-model, cross-seed challenge spanning prompting, fine-tuning, steering, sparse autoencoders, and editing, with tests of intervention composition and persistence after additional training.

Well-funded lab: Run a blinded, preregistered intervention tournament across model families in which one team predicts effects, another executes interventions, and an independent group evaluates hidden targets and side effects.

noveltyReview.scope: Targeted arXiv searches for mechanistic interpretability interventions, activation and representation steering, sparse-autoencoder steering, knowledge editing, causal localization, intervention side-effect prediction, SAEBench, AxBench, and 2025-2026 benchmark audits; reference chaining from the representative studies.
noveltyReview.note: High confidence that predictable, durable, composable control with bounded side effects remains open. There are meaningful local successes, so the claim is deliberately about calibrated ex ante prediction across methods and models, not whether interventions ever work. No priority claim is made.

counterexamples: AxBench provides a broad steering benchmark and finds prompting strongest overall, supervised fine-tuning next, and sparse autoencoders often uncompetitive; it is evidence both of controllability and of weak mechanistic advantage.
Causal localization can identify behaviorally relevant components, yet the localization-versus-editing study finds it does not consistently predict the most effective edit layer.
Recent work predicts some sparse-autoencoder steering side effects before intervention, but generalization varies across models, dictionaries, and target concepts.

literature.t: AxBench: Steering LLMs? Even Simple Baselines Outperform Sparse Autoencoders
Does Localization Inform Editing? Surprising Differences in Causality-Based Localization vs. Knowledge Editing in Language Models

benchmarks: CounterFact plus neighborhood tests and MQuAKE-style multi-hop edits
datasets: AxBench concept datasets and feature dictionaries
MQuAKE or an equivalent compositional-edit set

questions: Can enforceable least-privilege and containment policies for adaptive tool-using agents survive realistic prompt injection, delegation, persistence, privilege escalation, and sandbox-escape attacks?

direction.question: Can enforceable least-privilege and containment policies for adaptive tool-using agents survive realistic prompt injection, delegation, persistence, privilege escalation, and sandbox-escape attacks?
direction.closureCriteria: Specify the policy and threat model formally; enforce it below the model layer; test benign utility and adaptive attacks across real tool classes, delegation, memory, restart, identity, network, and code execution; show bounded failure probability under repeated trials; and obtain an independent penetration test.
partialResults: AI Control shows that monitoring and protocol design can improve safety even when an untrusted model intentionally subverts a coding task. AgentDojo and Agent Security Bench provide realistic tool-agent prompt-injection and security suites, while SandboxEscapeBench tests container-escape capability. These are substantial defenses and measurements, but none establishes general containment under an adaptive real-tool threat model.
starters: Individual: Add a deny-by-default, provenance-aware least-privilege wrapper to AgentDojo and compare it with prompt-only defenses on both benign utility and adaptive indirect prompt injection.

Small lab: Combine AgentDojo, Agent Security Bench, and sandbox-escape tasks in gVisor or Firecracker; red-team delegation, memory, restart, exfiltration, and privilege transitions across four model families.

Well-funded lab: Build an isolated replica of a real enterprise tool environment with formal identity, network, filesystem, and approval policies; commission independent model red teaming and a conventional penetration test.

noveltyReview.scope: Targeted arXiv searches for AI control, agent containment, agent security benchmarks, prompt injection, capability control, least privilege, tool authorization, container escape, adaptive red teaming, and 2024-2026 follow-on work; reference chaining from AI Control, AgentDojo, ASB, and SandboxEscapeBench.
noveltyReview.note: High confidence that enforceable containment surviving adaptive attacks in realistic tool environments remains open. Empirical defenses and control protocols are active and valuable, so the claim is not that no defenses exist. No universal impossibility or priority claim is made.

counterexamples: AI Control demonstrates that trusted monitoring, auditing, and protocol design improve outcomes against an intentionally subversive untrusted coding model, within a bounded backdoor-insertion setting.
AgentDojo contains 97 benign tasks and 629 security test cases across four tool domains; tested agents and defenses still trade off utility and security.
Agent Security Bench spans ten scenarios, more than 400 tools, and roughly 90,000 tests, while SandboxEscapeBench adds realistic container-escape tasks; neither alone proves containment.

estimated.wellFundedLab: Isolated replicas of real tools and identity systems, kernel and network specialists, formal-policy expertise, independent penetration testing, and incident-response capacity.

direction.tractability: High for benchmark and least-privilege improvements, medium for robust production patterns, and very low for broad formal containment guarantees.
